newsitem.title: INDIA: India says huge railway network starved of funds.
newsitem.headline: India says huge railway network starved of funds.

text.p: India said on Wednesday that its giant state-run railway network was in dire straits and its decades-old track system needed funds that were in short supply but stopped short of talk about privatisation.

"I have no hesitation in informing this august house that the Indian Railways are passing through a very difficult phase," Railway Minister Ram Vilas Paswan told parliament while unveiling the railway budget for 1997/98 (April-March).
India's rail network, which spans 62,000 km (38,750 miles) in terms of routes covered and 107,000 km (66,875 miles) in terms of track length, needed a 10 percent renewal of tracks, he said.
"In addition to this, replacement of 20,000 wagons, 2,000 coaches and many locomotives is required to be done every year due to over age," Paswan said.
"All these require enormous resources which are beyond the capacity of the railways."
India's railways has grown to be the largest in Asia and is the main mode of long-distance transport in the country of 936 million people.
Freight traffic is expected to contribute 67 percent of the railways' estimated net revenue of 37.56 billion rupees ($1.05 billion) in 1996/97 to March 31.
Paswan proposed a 12 percent hike in freight rates but exempted goods like grains, fuel and fertilisers, which could stoke inflation.
He proposed a 10 percent rise in first class passenger fares in the budget and a 5.0 percent rise in long-distance second class fares. The current Indian inflation rate is around 8.0 percent.

The budget proposed no hike in its development plan outlay for 1997/98, which represents the amount the government would spend on maintaining existing facilities or building new ones. The amount remained stationary at 83 billion rupees.

Starved of funds to grow, the railways would rely heavily on the issue of bonds by the Indian Railway Finance Corporation (IRFC) and private investors who are allowed to build some facilities or own wagons to carry their goods.

The IRFC would raise 21.5 billion rupees in 1997/98, up from 18.5 billion rupees in the current 1996/97. Private investors are expected to put in 9.0 billion rupees, up from 5.3 billion rupees in the current year.

The railways would raise 34.19 billion rupees from their own resources and get budgetary support from the government of 18.31 billion rupees in 1997/98, 4.0 billion rupees more than in the current fiscal year.

"The 12 percent freight raise will definitely create a problem for the common man," said Sharad Pawar, a key leader of the Congress party, which offers make-or-break support to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition.
